Saint-Bernard-de-Lacolle – À la rencontr: Saint-Bernard-de-Lacolle – Meeting the asylum seekers fleeing the United States
Saint-Bernard-de-Lacolle accueille de pl: Saint-Bernard-de-Lacolle is welcoming a growing number of asylum seekers from the United States. We met some of them.
Le poste frontalier de Saint-Bernard-de-: The Saint-Bernard-de-Lacolle border crossing. Photo: Loubna Chlaikhy
La Converse a choisi de réaliser un repo: La Converse chose to report from Saint-Bernard-de-Lacolle because, beyond the numbers, the political debates of the election campaign and the alarming headlines about immigration, there are faces, lives and human stories. This border crossing between Canada and the United States is becoming a new stage for the migration of asylum seekers fleeing the policies of the Trump administration.
Ce sont ces histoires que j’ai voulu rac: These are the stories I wanted to tell by going to meet the people arriving here with the hope of a fresh start. Meeting Hugues, Ketly and their family means hearing about the kilometres travelled, the nights in a processing centre, the suitcases dragged along at arm’s length, but also the family solidarity, the smiles despite the exhaustion, the dignity in the face of uncertainty.
J’ai aussi voulu rencontrer des résident: I also wanted to speak with residents of the surrounding area and with the mayor of Saint-Bernard-de-Lacolle, who have already witnessed the large-scale arrival of asylum seekers through Roxham Road.
Ce reportage ne vise pas à nier les enje: This report does not aim to deny the issues arising from border management or the challenges of welcoming newcomers, but to give a voice to those who bear the consequences of a situation over which they have no control.
Merci à celles et ceux qui ont accepté d: Thank you to those who agreed to share their stories with trust and sincerity.
<strong>Le poste frontalier de Saint-Ber: The Saint-Bernard-de-Lacolle border crossing is receiving a growing number of asylum seekers who want to leave the United States, where the Trump administration is threatening them with deportation. In the middle of a federal election, the fear of a new Roxham Road is at the heart of the debates. But behind the arrival of these migrants are just as many human beings, individual journeys, shattered dreams and hopes for a better life. La Converse went to Saint-Bernard-de-Lacolle to meet them. Report.
Sous le ciel nuageux de ce début de prin: Under the cloudy sky of early spring, all is calm around the Saint-Bernard-de-Lacolle border crossing. Nothing hints at what has been unfolding here for several weeks. Yet just a few metres away, near a large sign welcoming everyone arriving from the United States with “Welcome to Quebec,” is the asylum claims processing centre. No sign, no notice, nothing indicates that this concrete block – a grey, one-storey building – houses the asylum claims processing centre.
Mais rien ne bouge en ce début d’après-m: But nothing is moving this early afternoon. It is a far cry from the flow once seen at Roxham Road. The only comings and goings are those of security guards and police officers taking a break outside to smoke a cigarette or make a call.
Pourtant, Saint-Bernard-de-Lacolle est a: Still, Saint-Bernard-de-Lacolle is at the heart of the debates driving the federal election campaign in Canada. On April 8, Quebec’s immigration minister, Jean-François Roberge, stirred controversy by declaring: “Quebec cannot, on its own, take in all the misery of the world.” He said he did not wish to apologize for the remark, despite the criticism and despite the fact that the numbers show asylum claims are down 53 per cent from the previous year (see sidebar).
Depuis son élection, Donald Trump mène p: Since being elected, Donald Trump has been waging, for all intents and purposes, a hunt for migrants. Last month, the U.S. Department of Homeland Security decided to cancel the <l1>legal status granted to some 532,000 people</l1> from Cuba, Haiti, Nicaragua and Venezuela by the Biden administration. They recently learned that their status will end on April 24, 2025. A veritable earthquake for these populations seeking asylum.
Par ailleurs, l’administration Trump a d: The Trump administration has also said it wants to end Temporary Protected Status (TPS) for about 600,000 Venezuelans and 500,000 Haitians next August. That decision was, however, <l1>suspended</l1> by two federal judges in Texas and New York on April 9. A significant setback for the Republican president, who is dismantling, one by one, the programs put in place by his Democratic predecessor.
Mais cette décision de justice pourrait: But this court ruling could be only temporary, and many people targeted by these measures are looking for somewhere to take refuge. Canada thus appears to be the only way out.
Selon l’Agence des services frontaliers: According to the Canada Border Services Agency (CBSA), these announcements coincided with a sharp rise in the number of crossings at the Saint-Bernard-de-Lacolle port of entry. There were 560 asylum claims in January, 755 in February and 1,356 in March. From April 1<sup>st</sup> to 6, 557 claims were already received at this border crossing, compared with 171 claims from April 1<sup>st</sup> to 6, 2024.
<strong>De Boston à Montréal : le parcou: From Boston to Montréal: the journey of Hugues and his family, in search of a fresh start
Vers 19h, on perçoit enfin de l’agitatio: Around 7 p.m., there is finally some activity around the border crossing’s asylum claims processing centre. Several people come out through a gate. They hold transparent folders containing documents and drag their suitcases along at arm’s length. While some pile into cars that drive off right away, two people seem lost. They are Ketly and Hugues.
« Je suis venue chercher mes deux frères: “I came to pick up my two brothers, their wives, one of whom is pregnant, and my one-year-old niece. I took my pickup, but there isn’t room for everyone, so the two of us are going to take an Uber,” says Ketly, who has lived in Montréal for more than 30 years. Since I’m also heading back to Montréal, I offer to make the trip together.
« Avec plaisir, vous êtes notre bonne ét: “With pleasure, you’re our lucky star!” Ketly says enthusiastically as she gets into the car. “You can welcome him! This is my brother, and he just came out of the centre after two days of checks on his asylum claim! He has quite a story, he can tell you on the way if you like,” she explains, pointing to the young man settling into the back seat.
Malgré la fatigue, Hugues est ravi de ra: Despite his fatigue, Hugues is happy to tell his story. He left Boston three days ago with his wife and daughter and took the bus to Plattsburgh, where he met up with his older brother and sister-in-law. Together, they took a taxi to the Saint-Bernard-de-Lacolle border crossing – and covered the last kilometre on foot, dragging their eight suitcases. “We spent 36 hours in the centre. In fact, we celebrated my daughter’s first birthday yesterday,” says the 28-year-old Haitian man, in the light tone of someone describing his last trip to the movies.
Lorsqu’ils se présentent à la frontière,: When they arrive at the border, asylum seekers must go through several steps, for which some are better prepared than others. “I did my research beforehand, so they had all the birth certificates and documents proving I’m their sister so they could benefit from the exception. I was confident, I knew there wouldn’t be a problem,” Ketly says.
Ketly marche auprès de son frère Hugues: Ketly walks beside her brother Hugues, whom she has just picked up outside the asylum claims processing centre at the Saint-Bernard-de-Lacolle border crossing. Photo: Loubna Chlaikhy
Hugues avoue avoir été quelque peu inqui: Hugues admits he was a bit worried himself. After the first screening, the family was asked to leave their luggage in a room set aside for that purpose, and each person was given a wristband with a number. They were then called in for a first interview with a border officer. “They asked us a lot of questions about our situation, what we plan to do here… but nothing difficult. Then they took us to a big room with bunk beds everywhere; they gave each of us a sheet and something to eat. Not much, but it was enough,” says Hugues, who is keen to point out the kindness of the border officers.
Le centre de traitement fonctionne 24 he: The processing centre operates 24 hours a day to cope with the influx of claimants. The night is short, and there aren’t enough beds for everyone. The next day, during a second interview, a border officer calls Ketly in. “He asked me a lot of questions! They consider that I’m taking in five people, since the baby counts as an adult for them,” she says. The thought makes her burst out laughing.
« Il m’a demandé si j’étais vraiment sûr: “He asked me if I was really sure I wanted to take them all in. He said that for my brothers he understands, but with their wives, it’s maybe a lot for me. But I’m not going to tell my brothers to leave their wives behind! He wanted to know what I do for work, how I’m going to pay for everyone until they get their papers, where they’re going to live…” Ketly says. You can tell she takes her role as the eldest to heart and feels responsible for the success of her brothers’ immigration to Canada.
Il faut dire que son frère a déjà enduré: It must be said that her brother has already endured a long and difficult migration journey. In 2021, he tried for the first time to reach the United States by way of Brazil, then Mexico, on a month-long odyssey. Upon reaching the American border, he was placed in detention and sent back to Haiti. The following year, he took the same route and was held in U.S. immigration detention for a month. But this time, he was allowed to stay in the United States.
Depuis, il s’est installé à Boston, où v: Since then, he settled in Boston, where one of his cousins lives. He brought over his wife and had his first child. “I was an Uber driver there. But my wife received the letter from Immigration telling her to leave. Going back to Haiti isn’t possible, it’s too dangerous, I don’t want that for my daughter,” he says.
Arrivés à Montréal, Ketly, Hugues et leu: Back in Montréal, Ketly, Hugues and their family unload the suitcases they hope to pull out again only for vacations. Photo: Loubna Chlaikhy
Il est 20 h 30 lorsque nous arrivons dev: It is 8:30 p.m. when we arrive in front of Ketly’s apartment in north Montréal. Eyes full of wonder, Hugues discovers Montréal by night through the car window. By the time he gets out of the car, the van driven by his friend pulls up in turn. Exhaustion is written on the drawn faces of the other family members, who pull the suitcases out of the back. “They’re going to sleep well tonight!” Ketly says with a laugh.
Malheureusement, tous les demandeurs d’a: Unfortunately, not all asylum seekers are lucky enough to have a Ketly living in Canada. At the Saint-Bernard-de-Lacolle border crossing, some are forced to turn back.
<strong>580 demandeurs d’asile renvoyés: 580 asylum seekers sent back to the United States as of March 5, 2025
« Les agents de police sont débordés, ca: “The police officers are overwhelmed, because this wasn’t planned, but the reality is they’re stuck with it, and I think some officers are becoming impatient,” says Frantz André, a member of the Comité d’action des personnes sans statut (CAPSS). The organization works mainly with Haitian asylum seekers, who make up the majority of current arrivals, followed by Venezuelans. According to the activist, some run into obstacles when crossing the border at Saint-Bernard-de-Lacolle. As of March 5, 2025, 580 people had been sent back to the United States since the start of the year, according to the CBSA.
Les policiers de la GRC patrouillent le: RCMP officers patrol along the border. Photo: Loubna Chlaikhy
Frantz André raconte comment une famille: Frantz André describes how a family was allegedly separated for no reason last week. A couple and their six-year-old daughter were eligible for the family exception, says the activist, who helped the family prepare their file. But only the father was reportedly able to cross the border in the end, while his wife and daughter were allegedly turned back to the United States. “They told me the officer threatened to cancel their legal status in the U.S., when she has absolutely no power to do that!” he says indignantly.
Grâce au CAPSS, une chambre d’hôtel a ét: Thanks to CAPSS, a hotel room was paid for so the woman and child had somewhere to stay while a solution was found. They reportedly ended up crossing the border with the help of smugglers and are hiding right now. After two weeks on Canadian territory, she will be able to claim asylum in turn. “Smugglers make a lot of money, and we know there are cases of sexual abuse, for example. But people borrow money from their families or from loan sharks to try to ensure their survival, because we know that right now, there is a civil war in Haiti. These people have no choice,” the activist says. In his view, Canada has a moral responsibility toward Haiti and its people.
Une caméra de surveillance sur le chemin: A surveillance camera on Roxham Road. Photo: Loubna Chlaikhy
À l’instar de nombreux organismes comme: Like many organizations, including Amnesty International, Frantz André denounces the <l1>Safe Third Country Agreement</l1>. It applies along the entire land border and stipulates that a person must claim asylum in the first country deemed safe that they arrive in. Immigrants arriving from the United States are therefore not allowed to file a claim in Canada. There are, however, three exceptions: people who have a family member settled in Canada (parent, child, brother, sister), unaccompanied minors, and people who crossed the border irregularly and can prove they have been on Canadian territory for at least 14 days.
« Ma position, depuis plusieurs années,: “My position, for several years now, is that Canada should withdraw from this agreement, because we signed the Geneva Convention in 1969<sup>1</sup> and we are not honouring it. A safe country, normally, is a country where you are safe, and that is not the case for the United States,” he says.
Frantz André n’est pas le seul à se mobi: Frantz André is not the only one mobilizing. Near the border, a citizens’ committee has been active since 2017 to demand an end to this bilateral agreement.
<strong>À Saint-Bernard-de-Lacolle, les: In Saint-Bernard-de-Lacolle, residents waver between fear and solidarity
Il y a comme un air de déjà-vu pour les: There is a sense of déjà vu for residents of Saint-Bernard-de-Lacolle and the surrounding area. The streets are deserted this Thursday afternoon, but everyone knows what is happening not far away, at the border crossing. “For now, there are no consequences for the community, because everything is handled at the border services level,” says Estelle Muzzi, the municipality’s mayor.
Estelle Muzzi, mairesse de Saint-Bernard: Estelle Muzzi, mayor of Saint-Bernard-de-Lacolle, in front of City Hall. Photo: Loubna Chlaikhy
Selon l’élue, les municipalités situées: According to the mayor, municipalities near the border were approached by the federal and provincial governments as early as January. “We were told we could share our concerns with them and that RCMP staffing had been increased. There are a lot of patrols, and there are also unmarked cars driving around to see if there are smuggling networks. So they assure us that the border is very well secured,” explains M<sup>s</sup>. Muzzi.
Si la présence accrue des patrouilles de: While the increased presence of RCMP patrols reassures some residents, others oppose it. That is how the citizens’ committee Des Ponts pas des Frontières came into being in 2017, to express the community’s support for asylum seekers. “Everyone who lives near the border got a flyer at home telling them to alert the RCMP if they see someone,” the organization says. M<sup>s</sup>. Muzzi confirms this.
Policiers juchés sur des quads au milieu: Police officers perched on ATVs in the middle of a forest clearing, a helicopter in the sky in the background – the photo on the first page of the flyer, a copy of which La Converse obtained, looks straight out of an action movie. “As a citizen living near the border, you can help us identify any suspicious persons or situations in order to prevent various offences or any form of criminality,” it reads inside.
Le dépliant de la GRC distribué aux habi: The RCMP flyer distributed to residents near the border. Photo: reproduction
Une phrase qui irrite les militants. « D: A sentence that irritates activists. “This wording amounts to lumping asylum seekers in with criminals, and that’s not right. It needs to be said that even those who cross the border irregularly, meaning at an unofficial point of entry, are not breaking the law under Canadian and international law,” they explain. The “examples of suspicious situations” the RCMP invites people to report are also surprising: “people are evasive about their destination,” “people walking with a backpack or suitcases,” or even “a vehicle you don’t recognize.” The organization refuses to take part in this kind of measure and says many residents are themselves stopped and checked on a regular basis.
« De nouvelles caméras de surveillance o: “New surveillance cameras have been installed on several roads, and some of us get stopped by the RCMP for no reason at all. All of this creates fear among some people, who call the RCMP as soon as they see someone near their home,” says one member. “For me, this is not a way to treat people who are fleeing a country that is threatening us; it’s unthinkable!”
Des caméras de surveillance sont en effe: Surveillance cameras are indeed visible on several roads, and the RCMP stopped our vehicle twice while we were preparing this report.
De son côté, Estelle Muzzi se refuse à c: For her part, Estelle Muzzi declines to comment on questions of international politics. Seated at the large wooden council table in City Hall, she nevertheless wants to express her solidarity. “I have a lot of compassion for these migrants. All they want is to be able to live and work in safety. These are people who had legal status and who had integrated, but Trump wiped all that out,” says the mayor, who mentions her Italian roots. “I don’t know how all this is going to end, but above all it’s human misery. It’s not easy for anyone, even for the border officers. I imagine it must be heartbreaking for them to turn someone away.”
Alors que le Canada est en pleine campag: With Canada in the middle of a federal election campaign, several political parties have seized on the migration issue.
<strong>L’immigration au cœur de la camp: Immigration at the heart of the election campaign
Le chef bloquiste Yves-François Blanchet: Bloc Québécois leader Yves-François Blanchet is the only politician to have visited the Saint-Bernard-de-Lacolle border crossing, last Thursday. “The federal government has completely abdicated its responsibilities when it comes to border management. (...) The border is a sieve, to the point that the Quebec government recently sent the Sûreté du Québec there to do Ottawa’s job,” he said at a press conference.
Le Bloc québécois a annoncé à cette occa: On that occasion, the Bloc Québécois announced that it is proposing the creation of a Minister of Borders position to head the Canada Border Services Agency. The party also wants to end the 14-day exception in the Safe Third Country Agreement, toughen penalties for smugglers and authorize border officers to patrol outside border crossings to help the RCMP.
Du côté du Parti libéral, Mark Carney se: On the Liberal side, Mark Carney is taking shelter behind the Agreement and wants ineligible asylum seekers to be sent back to the United States. The current prime minister dismissed the Bloc’s proposal for a border ministry: “We have just [deployed] drones, more staff and more helicopters, and it’s working. So I don’t think it’s a good idea to create a new ministry.” The Liberal government did in fact launch a $1.3-billion plan to strengthen border security in late 2024.
Le candidat conservateur Pierre Poilievr: Conservative candidate Pierre Poilievre, for his part, wants to sort the good asylum seekers from the bad. “If [the person] can prove they are a genuine asylum seeker, with no criminal record, and that they can contribute to our country, they should be able to stay here,” he said during a stop in Edmonton on April 8. He did, however, blame the housing, employment and even health crises on a hypothetical “massive fraud involving international students, foreign workers and fake asylum seekers.”
Une sortie qui a suscité la polémique lo: The remark stirred controversy when some media outlets revealed that the uncle of Anaida Poilievre, the Conservative leader’s wife, crossed the Canadian border on foot twice – in 2004, then in 2018 via Roxham Road, after his asylum claim was rejected in 2005. The New Democratic Party and the Green Party of Canada did not respond to our requests.
Quoi qu’il en soit, Hugues et sa famille: Whatever the case, Hugues and his family want to stay positive and believe in a fresh start, the right one this time. “Canada was my dream, to be near my sister. I’m ready to start everything over here, like I did in the United States,” the young man says, like a promise to himself.

Malgré le ton alarmiste de certains poli: Despite the alarmist tone of some politicians and commentators in recent weeks, the number of asylum claims received since the start of 2025 is down compared with the same period in 2024. Airports were then the main point of entry for claimants. Border officers had processed 5,246 asylum claims as of April 6, 2025, compared with 11,118 on the same date last year, a drop of about 53 per cent.
Ottawa a en effet durci les règles d’imm: Ottawa has indeed tightened immigration rules at airports. In February 2024, a visa became mandatory for some Mexican nationals, who were arriving in large numbers as tourists and claiming asylum on arrival at the airport. The Trudeau government also made it harder for Indian nationals to obtain tourist visas. Today, the land border is therefore the main point of entry for asylum seekers.
Le Plan frontalier lancé par le gouverne: The Border Plan launched by the Trudeau government in December 2024 also sets removal targets. “The CBSA has increased the number of removals of people inadmissible to Canada, [which is] the highest in a decade,” the agency points out. Canada plans to maintain current removal levels for 2025 and to increase them by 25 per cent in the following years.
